clinicalPearls: BCG is a live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis strain, so dissemination reflects a failure of host containment rather than an unusually virulent organism.
Two populations dominate: infants with underlying primary immunodeficiency who receive the vaccine, and adults treated with intravesical BCG for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

In an infant, disseminated BCG may be the sentinel presentation of severe combined immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, or a defect in the IL-12/IFN-gamma (Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease) axis.
Intravesical BCG complications form a spectrum from local cystitis and granulomatous prostatitis to epididymo-orchitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis and miliary spread.
Traumatic catheterisation, instillation into an inflamed or bleeding bladder, or early instillation after resection predispose to systemic absorption.
M. bovis BCG is intrinsically resistant to pyrazinamide, which distinguishes its treatment from that of M. tuberculosis.
A systemic hypersensitivity-type reaction to mycobacterial antigens may coexist with true infection, and corticosteroids are sometimes added to antimycobacterial therapy.
Mycobacterial culture is slow, so treatment is frequently begun empirically on clinical and radiological grounds while confirmation is awaited.
reference.pathophysiology: BCG is a live attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis. After vaccination or intravesical instillation the organism is normally contained by an intact cell-mediated response that depends on macrophage-lymphocyte cross-talk through the IL-12/IL-23/IFN-gamma axis. Dissemination arises when this containment fails, either because the host is immunodeficient (severe combined immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, or Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease from defects in genes such as IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1 and NEMO) or because a large mycobacterial load gains direct vascular access, as when bacilli are absorbed across a traumatised or inflamed urothelium during intravesical therapy. Once bloodborne, the bacilli seed reticuloendothelial organs and produce granulomatous inflammation in the liver, spleen, bone marrow, lungs and genitourinary tract. Part of the clinical illness reflects an immune-mediated hypersensitivity response to mycobacterial antigens rather than uncontrolled bacterial replication, which is why some patients improve with corticosteroids given alongside antimycobacterial drugs.
additionalDifferentials: Miliary or disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
Recurrent or metastatic bladder cancer in patients treated with intravesical BCG
Lymphoma or other haematological malignancy presenting with fever, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias
Sepsis of other bacterial or fungal origin
additionalInvestigations: Mycobacterial blood cultures together with cultures of urine, bone marrow and affected tissue
Acid-fast staining and mycobacterial culture of biopsy material (liver, marrow, bladder or prostate)
Molecular identification to distinguish M. bovis BCG from the wider M. tuberculosis complex
Immunological work-up in infants, including lymphocyte subsets, a neutrophil oxidative-burst test for chronic granulomatous disease, and IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway genetics
Cross-sectional imaging of chest and abdomen for organ involvement and a miliary pattern
Liver function tests and inflammatory markers
redFlags: Persistent fever, weight loss and hepatosplenomegaly after intravesical BCG or in a recently vaccinated infant
Features of miliary spread such as respiratory compromise with diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
Cytopenias suggesting marrow involvement or a haemophagocytic process
Vascular involvement, including mycotic aneurysm following intravesical therapy
Failure to thrive with recurrent infections in an infant, pointing to an underlying immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and prolonged multidrug antimycobacterial therapy, localised or moderate disease generally does well. Disseminated disease, particularly in profoundly immunodeficient infants, carries substantial mortality unless the underlying immune defect is corrected, for example by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
pitfalls: Prescribing pyrazinamide, to which M. bovis BCG is intrinsically resistant, on the assumption the organism behaves like M. tuberculosis.
Attributing post-instillation fever purely to a benign reaction and thereby missing true dissemination.
Failing to investigate for an underlying immunodeficiency when an infant develops BCG disease.
Delaying therapy while awaiting slow mycobacterial culture confirmation.
Overlooking genitourinary or vascular foci such as granulomatous prostatitis or a mycotic aneurysm.
references: Urological oncology guidance on intravesical therapy
management: Prolonged multidrug antimycobacterial therapy is the mainstay, using isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol while recognising the intrinsic pyrazinamide resistance of Mycobacterium bovis BCG
Stop intravesical BCG instillation and give no further doses after a systemic reaction
Add corticosteroids for severe or hypersensitivity-type reactions to intravesical BCG
Investigate and correct the underlying immunodeficiency in infants, such as severe combined immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, or an IL-12/IFN-gamma axis defect
Consider IFN-gamma therapy and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation where a correctable immune defect is identified
Provide supportive care for organ involvement such as hepatitis and pneumonitis and for sepsis
Prevent systemic absorption by avoiding traumatic catheterisation and delaying instillation after transurethral resection
Involve infectious diseases and immunology, and offer genetic counselling where a heritable immunodeficiency is confirmed
